works.title: Il pastor fido
works.subtitle: Tragicommedia pastorale
works.author: Battista Guarini
works.blurb: Guarini's pastoral tragicomedy of Arcadia, first printed in 1590: the shepherd Mirtillo loves the nymph Amarilli, who is promised to Silvio, a hunter who scorns love, while an oracle demands the sacrifice of a faithful maiden to end the land's ancient curse. Written in emulation of Tasso's Aminta, it was among the most widely read secular works in Europe for almost two centuries.

works.title: Patience
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.blurb: A retelling of the Book of Jonah in about 530 alliterative lines, preceded by a prologue on the Beatitudes of poverty and patience. The reluctant prophet flees by sea, is swallowed by the whale and is finally rebuked for his anger at God's mercy.

works.title: Patience
works.subtitle: Or, Bunthorne's Bride
works.author: W. S. Gilbert
works.blurb: The rapturous maidens of Castle Bunthorne all adore the fleshly poet Reginald Bunthorne, until the idyllic poet Archibald Grosvenor arrives and draws their devotion away from him. Between the two aesthetes stands Patience, the simple milkmaid, who is wooed by both and must work out what unselfish love really means.

works.title: Paulicéia desvairada
works.author: Mário de Andrade
works.blurb: The first modernist book of verse in Brazil, a sequence of free-verse poems on São Paulo. Poems from the 1922 first edition (S. Paulo, Casa Mayença), in the original spelling, as far as proofread transcription exists.

works.title: Description of Greece, Books I-II (Loeb)
works.subtitle: Attica and Corinth
works.author: Pausanias
works.blurb: The first two books of the traveller Pausanias's Greek guidebook, Attica and Corinth, with their temples, statues, legends and battles, in W. H. S. Jones's Loeb translation of 1918.

works.title: Description of Greece, Books III-V (Loeb)
works.subtitle: Laconia, Messenia and Elis
works.author: Pausanias
works.translator: trans. W. H. S. Jones and H. A. Ormerod (1926)
works.blurb: Pausanias's guidebook through Laconia, Messenia and the first part of Elis, with Sparta's shrines, the Messenian wars and the Olympic sanctuary, in the Loeb translation of W. H. S. Jones and H. A. Ormerod (1926).

works.title: Description of Greece, vol. 1 (Books I-VI)
works.subtitle: Attica, Corinth, Laconia, Messenia and Elis
works.author: Pausanias
works.blurb: The first half of the traveller Pausanias's Greek guidebook: Attica, Corinth, Laconia, Messenia and Elis, with their temples, statues, legends and battles, in A. R. Shilleto's English of 1886.

works.title: Description of Greece, vol. 2 (Books VII-X)
works.subtitle: Achaia, Arcadia, Boeotia and Phocis
works.author: Pausanias
works.blurb: The second half of the traveller Pausanias's Greek guidebook: Achaia, Arcadia, Boeotia and Phocis, with their temples, statues, legends and battles, in A. R. Shilleto's English of 1886.

works.title: Pearl
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.blurb: A grieving father falls asleep on the grave of his infant daughter and dreams her transfigured into a maiden of Heaven, radiant among the elect — an elegy of loss answered by consolation, in interlocking rhymed stanzas.

works.title: Pearl (Middle English text)
works.subtitle: The Pearl
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.blurb: The original Middle English text of the dream-vision elegy, in 101 twelve-line stanzas of interlocking rhyme and alliteration. A bereaved father falls asleep by the grave of his lost pearl and sees her, transfigured, across a stream in the heavenly city.

works.title: Peer Gynt
works.subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
works.author: Henrik Ibsen
works.blurb: Peer Gynt, a boastful young peasant, steals a bride, flees into the mountains and the hall of the Troll King, and goes out into the world: a rich trader in Morocco, a prophet among the Bedouin, an emperor in a Cairo madhouse. Returning old and empty-handed, he meets the Button-Moulder, who has come to melt him down, and the faithful Solveig, who has waited.

works.title: The Psalms of David (Psalms 44–150)
works.subtitle: Metrical paraphrase from the Sidney Psalter, in the 1823 printed text
works.author: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.blurb: The Countess of Pembroke's verse paraphrase of Psalms 44–150, each psalm in a different stanza form, completing the psalter begun by her brother Sir Philip Sidney.

works.title: Perceval ou le Conte du Graal
works.subtitle: Le Roman de Perceval; Li Contes del Graal
works.author: Chrétien de Troyes
works.blurb: Chrétien's last, unfinished Arthurian romance and the first story of the Grail, in which the naive young Perceval is knighted and fails to ask the question at the Fisher King's castle.

works.title: Pericles, Prince of Tyre
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.blurb: To make a wife of the incestuous Antiochus's daughter, Prince Pericles of Tyre must solve a deadly riddle, and having solved it he flees, beginning years of shipwreck and exile narrated by the ghostly poet Gower. He wins Thaisa at Pentapolis, loses her at sea in childbirth, and leaves their daughter Marina at Tarsus, where jealous Dionyza plots her murder and pirates carry her to a brothel in Mytilene. After a long grief he is reunited with Marina and, guided by Diana, with Thaisa at Ephesus.

works.title: Πέρσαι (Persai)
works.author: Aeschylus
works.blurb: The Greek text of this tragedy by Aeschylus in the Smyth Loeb edition, set out by episode and choral division, so that it can be read beside the English verse translation of the same play.

works.title: The Persians
works.author: Aeschylus
works.blurb: At the Persian court of Susa, the elders and the queen mother Atossa wait anxiously for news of Xerxes and his vast army, gone to conquer Greece. A messenger arrives with the tale of Salamis and the ruin of the fleet, and the ghost of Darius is raised from the tomb to name the king's pride as the cause. Xerxes returns in rags to a chorus of lament.

works.title: Peru
works.subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
works.author: Helen Maria Williams
works.blurb: A poem in six cantos on the Spanish conquest of Peru, the fall of the Inca Ataliba and the sufferings of his queen Alzira, ending in an appeal against cruelty and the lust for gold.

works.title: Песня про царя Ивана Васильевича, молодого опричника и удалого купца Калашникова (Pesnya pro kuptsa Kalashnikova)
works.subtitle: in the original Russian
works.author: Mikhail Lermontov
works.blurb: Lermontov's poem in the manner of the folk bylina: in the Moscow of Ivan the Terrible the merchant Kalashnikov fights the Tsar's favourite oprichnik to avenge the insult to his wife, in its original Russian.

works.title: Petits Poèmes en prose (Le Spleen de Paris)
works.subtitle: in the original French
works.author: Charles Baudelaire
works.blurb: Fifty short prose poems of Paris, written from the 1850s until the poet’s death: wandering, boredom, charity, vice and tenderness in the modern city. Baudelaire called them a serpent that may be cut anywhere.

works.title: The Satyricon
works.subtitle: Satyricon, or the Satyrical Adventures of Encolpius
works.author: Petronius
works.blurb: The surviving episodes of Petronius's comic novel of Nero's Italy, in which Encolpius and his companions drift from lodging-house to the banquet of the freedman Trimalchio, in Michael Heseltine's English prose of 1913.

works.title: Phaedra
works.author: Jean Racine
works.blurb: At Troezen, Phaedra, wife of the absent Theseus, wastes away with a guilty passion for her stepson Hippolytus. Word comes that Theseus is dead, and she confesses her love; then he returns alive. Her nurse Oenone accuses Hippolytus of the very crime Phaedra herself desired, and Theseus calls down Neptune's curse on his son, who is killed by a sea monster. Phaedra takes poison and admits her guilt before she dies.

works.title: Phaedra
works.subtitle: The Latin original
works.author: Seneca
works.blurb: Phaedra, consumed by love for her stepson Hippolytus, is spurned; she accuses him falsely to Theseus, and Hippolytus is destroyed.

works.title: Phaedra
works.subtitle: or Hippolytus
works.author: Seneca
works.blurb: Phaedra, wife of the absent Theseus, is consumed by a guilty passion for her stepson Hippolytus, an austere young huntsman who scorns love. Her nurse carries her secret to him and he recoils in horror. When Theseus unexpectedly returns, Phaedra accuses Hippolytus of attacking her. Theseus calls down a curse on his son, and a monster from the sea destroys him. Phaedra confesses the truth and kills herself.

works.title: Φαινόμενα (Phainomena)
works.author: Aratus
works.blurb: Aratus’s hexameter account of the constellations, the celestial circles, the risings and settings of the zodiac, and the signs of the weather, the most widely read poem of the Greek star-lore tradition. The Greek text is given here in Maass’s edition, so that it pairs with the English translations of the same poem.

works.title: The Phenomena and Diosemeia
works.author: Aratus of Soli
works.blurb: A heroic-couplet version of Aratus’s star-poem and its weather signs by John Lamb, Dean of Bristol, published in 1848.

works.title: Phaenomena
works.author: Aratus
works.blurb: Aratus’s hexameter account of the constellations, the celestial circles, the risings of the zodiac and the weather signs, a poem of the stars that was widely read and translated in antiquity.

sections.title: A. Constellations north of the ecliptic (Lines 19–318)
B. Constellations south of the ecliptic (Lines 319–453)
D. Circles of the celestial sphere (Lines 462–558)

works.title: Pharonnida
works.subtitle: A Heroick Poem
works.author: William Chamberlayne
works.blurb: A heroic romance in rhymed couplets, in five books of five cantos each, of love and adventure among Christians and Turks; text from the 1659 edition (EEBO-TCP), in original spelling.

works.title: Pharsalia
works.subtitle: De Bello Civili (The Civil War)
works.author: Lucan
works.blurb: Lucan’s unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey, notable for banishing the gods from its narrative entirely.

works.title: The Civil War (Pharsalia)
works.subtitle: Books I-X, Loeb translation by J. D. Duff
works.author: Lucan
works.blurb: J. D. Duff's plain prose translation of Lucan's unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Caesar and Pompey, ten books ending where Lucan's text breaks off.

works.title: Pharsalia
works.subtitle: Lucan's Pharsalia, containing the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey
works.author: Lucan
works.blurb: Sir Arthur Gorges's 1614 rhymed translation of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war, in octosyllabic couplets, with a verse argument before each book.

works.title: Pharsalia (Bellum civile)
works.subtitle: The Latin original
works.author: Lucan
works.blurb: Lucan's Latin epic of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey in ten books, in the original hexameters.

works.title: Pharsalia (May)
works.subtitle: Lucans Pharsalia: or The Civill Warres of Rome, betweene Pompey the Great, and Iulius Caesar
works.author: Lucan
works.blurb: Thomas May's rhymed heroic-couplet translation of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war, the first complete English version in pentameter couplets, with May's own verse argument before each book.

works.title: Pharsalia (Rowe)
works.subtitle: Lucan's Pharsalia, translated into English verse by Nicholas Rowe
works.author: Lucan
works.blurb: Nicholas Rowe's version of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war between Caesar and Pompey, in heroic couplets, published after the translator's death in 1718.

works.title: Philip van Artevelde: A Dramatic Romance
works.subtitle: In Two Parts
works.author: Sir Henry Taylor
works.blurb: Henry Taylor's blank-verse drama of the Ghent rebellion of the 1380s. In Part the First the scholar Philip van Artevelde, son of a famous father, is drawn from retirement to lead the White-Hoods of Ghent against the Earl of Flanders, and rises to power at Bruges. In Part the Second, now Regent of Flanders, he loves the Italian lady Elena and leads the Flemish host against the French king's army, and the play ends on the field of Roosebeke.

works.title: Philoctetes
works.author: Sophocles
works.blurb: Odysseus brings the young Neoptolemus to Lemnos to trick the exiled Philoctetes out of the bow of Heracles, without which Troy cannot fall. Neoptolemus, moved by pity and shame, gives the bow back, and only the appearance of the deified Heracles persuades the wounded archer to sail for Troy and healing.

works.title: Φιλοκτήτης (Philoktetes)
works.author: Sophocles
works.blurb: Odysseus and Neoptolemos come to Lemnos to fetch the abandoned archer Philoktetes and his bow, without which Troy cannot fall. Neoptolemos' conscience turns the trick of deceit into a test of honour. The Greek text is given in the order of the Storr edition, so that it pairs with the English prose translation of the same play.

works.title: Philoctetes
works.author: Sophocles
works.blurb: Left on desolate Lemnos for ten years with a festering wound, the archer Philoctetes is the only man who can bend the bow of Heracles, and Troy cannot fall without it. Odysseus sends young Neoptolemus to win the weapon by deceit, but the boy finds he cannot betray a suffering man, and only the voice of the deified Heracles can resolve the clash of honour and necessity.

works.title: The Tragedy of Philotas
works.author: Samuel Daniel
works.blurb: Daniel's tragedy of the fall of Philotas, son of Parmenio and the most admired of Alexander's Macedonian captains. Vain and free-spoken, he lets fall contemptuous words about the young king to his mistress Antigona; she is made to betray them, and when he fails to pass on warning of a plot against Alexander he is arraigned, put to torture and condemned. Choruses of three Greeks and a Persian close the acts. The play opens with a verse dedication to Prince Henry.

works.title: The Phoenician Maidens
works.author: Euripides
works.blurb: Thebes is besieged by Polyneikes and his Argive host, and the house of Oedipus stands on the edge of its last catastrophe: Jocasta, Kreon, the blind seer Teiresias and a chorus of Phoenician maidens watch as the brothers move toward single combat. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse.

works.title: Φοίνισσαι (Phoinissai)
works.author: Euripides
works.blurb: Thebes is under siege: Eteokles and Polyneikes, the sons of Oedipus, are at war over the city, and their mother Iokaste tries in vain to reconcile them at a meeting before the seven gates. The seer Teiresias then declares that Thebes can be saved only if Kreon's son Menoikeus is sacrificed, and the young man goes to his death for the city. The brothers kill each other in single combat and Iokaste takes her own life over their bodies. The blinded Oedipus is led into exile by his daughter Antigone, and the Greek text is given here in the order and bracketing of Nauck's Teubner edition, so that it pairs with Arthur Way's English verse translation.

works.title: Phoenissae
works.subtitle: The Latin original
works.author: Seneca
works.blurb: The blind Oedipus, led by Antigone, seeks death while Jocasta tries to reconcile their warring sons Eteocles and Polynices; the fragmentary play breaks off unfinished.

works.title: The Phoenix
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)
works.blurb: A richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

works.title: The Phoenix (Old English)
works.subtitle: Old English text
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.blurb: The Old English verse of a richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

works.title: The Piccolomini
works.author: Friedrich Schiller
works.blurb: At Pilsen, in the Thirty Years' War, the imperial generals gather round their commander Wallenstein while a plot against him is already being laid by Octavio Piccolomini, whose son Max loves Wallenstein's daughter Thekla. Octavio holds a secret commission to take the generalship, and father and son are drawn toward a collision of loyalties.

works.title: The Pierrot of the Minute
works.subtitle: A Dramatic Fantasy in One Act
works.author: Ernest Dowson
works.blurb: In a glade of the Petit Trianon a lovesick Pierrot, following a trail of lilies, sleeps before the statue of Cupid and is visited by a Moon Maiden, who grants him one night of love and a dream of it to take away at dawn. A one-act fantasy in rhymed couplets, with songs, and Dowson's most delicate stage piece.

works.title: Piers Plowman
works.subtitle: The Vision of Piers Ploughman
works.author: William Langland
works.blurb: Falling asleep on the Malvern Hills, the dreamer Will sees a field full of folk and sets out through a sequence of visions to find Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a vast alliterative satire of church, court, and commons.

works.title: The Pilgrims of the Sun
works.author: James Hogg
works.blurb: A visionary poem in four books, in Spenserian stanzas, in which a Scottish girl, Mary Lee, is borne in spirit through the planets and the sun, with a dedication to Lord Byron.

works.title: Pippa Passes
works.subtitle: A Drama
works.author: Robert Browning
works.blurb: Browning's drama of New Year's Day at Asolo follows Pippa, a silk-mill girl on her one holiday, whose songs, passing unheard by, break in on four scenes of love, guilt, plot and temptation and change the lives of those who hear them.

works.title: The Pirates of Penzance
works.subtitle: Or, The Slave of Duty
works.author: W. S. Gilbert
works.blurb: Frederic, bound apprentice to a band of tender-hearted pirates by his nurse's mistake, is freed on his twenty-first birthday and falls in love with Mabel, daughter of Major-General Stanley. But he was born on 29 February, so his indentures have barely a quarter of their term run, and his duty to the pirates and to the law pull him apart until a call to yield in Queen Victoria's name resolves the matter.

works.title: Alcibiades II
works.subtitle: The dialogue on prayer and the knowledge of what is good
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: On his way to pray, the young Alcibiades is asked by Socrates whether he knows what to ask of the gods; the talk turns to the danger of praying for evils in the belief that they are goods, and to the knowledge of the good that alone makes a prayer safe.

works.title: Apology
works.subtitle: The defence of Socrates before the Athenian jury
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates' speech to the Athenian jury at his trial for impiety and corrupting the young, followed by his words after the verdict and the sentence of death. Plato's account of the philosopher's defence of the examined life.

works.title: Apology
works.subtitle: The defence of Socrates before the Athenian jury
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates' speech to the Athenian jury at his trial for impiety and corrupting the young, followed by his words after the verdict and the sentence of death. Plato's account of the philosopher's defence of the examined life.

works.title: Charmides
works.subtitle: Socrates, Charmides and Critias on temperance
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Back from the siege of Potidaea, Socrates visits the palaestra of Taureas and meets the beautiful young Charmides. Together with Critias they ask what temperance is, and each definition in turn collapses, leaving the question open.

works.title: Charmides
works.subtitle: Socrates, Charmides and Critias on temperance
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Back from the siege of Potidaea, Socrates visits the palaestra of Taureas and meets the beautiful young Charmides. Together with Critias they ask what temperance is, and each definition in turn collapses, leaving the question open.

works.title: Cratylus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the correctness of names
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Hermogenes and Cratylus disagree whether names are natural or conventional; Socrates tests both views through a long run of etymologies, and ends by doubting that names can teach us the truth of things.

works.title: Cratylus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the correctness of names
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Hermogenes and Cratylus disagree whether names are natural or conventional; Socrates tests both views through a long run of etymologies, and ends by doubting that names can teach us the truth of things.

works.title: Critias
works.subtitle: The unfinished dialogue on ancient Athens and Atlantis
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Critias tells how ancient Athens and the island empire of Atlantis once stood against each other, in Bury's Loeb translation of the dialogue that breaks off in mid-speech.

works.title: Critias
works.subtitle: The unfinished dialogue on ancient Athens and Atlantis
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Critias tells how ancient Athens and the island empire of Atlantis once stood against each other, in a dialogue that breaks off in mid-speech.

works.title: Crito
works.subtitle: Socrates in prison refuses to escape
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: In the prison at dawn, Crito urges the condemned Socrates to escape. Socrates replies by questioning him on justice and, speaking for the Laws of Athens, explains why he must stay and accept his sentence.

works.title: Crito
works.subtitle: Socrates in prison refuses to escape
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: In the prison at dawn, Crito urges the condemned Socrates to escape. Socrates replies by questioning him on justice and, speaking for the Laws of Athens, explains why he must stay and accept his sentence.

works.title: Epinomis
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: A sequel to the Laws: the Athenian Stranger, the Cretan Cleinias and the Spartan Megillus ask what mortals must learn in order to be wise, and find the answer in number, the study of the heavens and the stars, and the piety that follows from knowing the orderly motions of the gods.

works.title: Euthydemus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the sophists and the art of wisdom
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates tells Crito how two sophist brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, tied a young man in knots with verbal tricks, and how he answered them by urging the young Cleinias to seek true wisdom.

works.title: Euthydemus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the sophists and the art of wisdom
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates tells Crito how two sophist brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, tied a young man in knots with verbal tricks, and how he answered them by urging the young Cleinias to seek true wisdom.

works.title: Euthyphro
works.subtitle: Socrates and Euthyphro on the nature of piety
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: On the porch of the King Archon, Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is about to prosecute his own father for murder, and asks him what piety really is. Each definition falls apart under questioning, and the dialogue ends without an answer.

works.title: Euthyphro
works.subtitle: Socrates and Euthyphro on the nature of piety
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: On the porch of the King Archon, Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is about to prosecute his own father for murder, and asks him what piety really is. Each definition falls apart under questioning, and the dialogue ends without an answer.

works.title: Gorgias
works.subtitle: Socrates on rhetoric, justice and the good life
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates questions the rhetoricians Gorgias and Polus, and then the ambitious Callicles, on whether the orator's power is a true art or mere flattery, and whether it is better to do wrong or to suffer it. Ends with the myth of the judgment of the dead.

works.title: Gorgias
works.subtitle: Socrates on rhetoric, justice and the good life
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates questions the rhetoricians Gorgias and Polus, and then the ambitious Callicles, on whether the orator's power is a true art or mere flattery, and whether it is better to do wrong or to suffer it. Ends with the myth of the judgment of the dead.

works.title: Hippias Major
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the nature of the beautiful
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates presses the sophist Hippias of Elis to say what the beautiful itself is, and one confident definition after another gives way under his questioning.

works.title: Hippias Minor
works.subtitle: On whether the man who errs willingly is better than the man who errs unwillingly
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: After Hippias of Elis has given a display on Homer, Socrates presses him on whether Achilles or Odysseus is the better man, and the talk turns to the paradox that one who lies or does wrong on purpose may be better than one who does so unwittingly. A short dialogue between Socrates, Hippias and Eudicus.

works.title: Ion
works.subtitle: The dialogue on inspiration and the rhapsode
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates questions the rhapsode Ion, a celebrated reciter of Homer, and argues that his gift comes not from art or knowledge but from divine inspiration, like a chain of magnets.

works.title: Ion
works.subtitle: The dialogue on inspiration and the rhapsode
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates questions the rhapsode Ion, a celebrated reciter of Homer, and argues that his gift comes not from art or knowledge but from divine inspiration, like a chain of magnets.

works.title: Laches
works.subtitle: The dialogue on courage
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Two fathers ask two generals how their sons should be educated; Socrates turns the question to courage, and no definition survives.

works.title: Laches
works.subtitle: Socrates, Laches and Nicias on the nature of courage
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Two Athenian fathers ask the generals Laches and Nicias, and then Socrates, whether their sons should learn fighting in armour. The question widens into a search for what courage is, and the dialogue ends without a definition.

works.title: Laws
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Plato's last and longest dialogue: an Athenian Stranger, a Cretan and a Spartan walk from Knossos to the cave of Zeus, talking the whole way, and draw up the laws of a new colony, from education, marriage and drinking parties to crime, religion and the Nocturnal Council that is to guard the state.

works.title: Laws
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Plato's last and longest dialogue: an Athenian Stranger, a Cretan and a Spartan walk from Knossos to the cave of Zeus, talking the whole way, and draw up the laws of a new colony, from education, marriage and drinking parties to crime, religion and the Nocturnal Council that is to guard the state.

works.title: Letters
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Thirteen letters transmitted under Plato's name, most of them touching his dealings with Dionysius of Syracuse and with Dion, his friend and pupil. The long Seventh Letter tells the story of Plato's three Sicilian journeys and sets out, in a famous digression, his view of what can and cannot be written down about the highest matters.

works.title: Lovers
works.subtitle: The dialogue on philosophy and the love of learning
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates, visiting a grammar school, overhears two rival lovers quarrelling over philosophy and an athlete, and questions them on what philosophizing is: much learning, or knowing what is of use and what a man needs for the good of his soul.

works.title: Lysis
works.subtitle: The dialogue on friendship
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates, on his way to the Lyceum, is drawn into a new palaestra and questions two young friends, Lysis and Menexenus, about what a friend is; the search ends without an answer.

works.title: Menexenus
works.subtitle: Socrates recites the funeral oration he learned from Aspasia
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates mocks the Athenian funeral oration, then recites one he says Aspasia taught him: a long panegyric of Athens from its mythic origins through the Persian and Peloponnesian wars.

works.title: Menexenus
works.subtitle: Socrates recites the funeral oration he learned from Aspasia
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates mocks the Athenian funeral oration, then recites one he says Aspasia taught him: a long panegyric of Athens from its mythic origins through the Persian and Peloponnesian wars.

works.title: Meno
works.subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Meno asks whether virtue can be taught; Socrates answers with a geometry lesson for a slave boy, the theory of recollection, and a search for what virtue is.

works.title: Meno
works.subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Meno asks whether virtue can be taught; Socrates answers with a geometry lesson for a slave boy, the theory of recollection, and a search for what virtue is.

works.title: Parmenides
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the One and the Forms
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Cephalus recounts how the young Socrates met the aged Parmenides and Zeno, and how Parmenides tested the theory of Forms and then led the young Aristoteles through the long exercise on the One.

works.title: Parmenides
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the One and the Forms
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Cephalus recounts how the young Socrates met the aged Parmenides and Zeno, and how Parmenides tested the theory of Forms and then led the young Aristoteles through the long exercise on the One.

works.title: Phaedo
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the death of Socrates
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: On his last day in prison Socrates talks with his friends about death, the soul and its survival, and then drinks the hemlock. Phaedo tells the story to Echecrates of Phlius.

works.title: Phaedo
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the death of Socrates
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: On his last day in prison Socrates talks with his friends about death, the soul and its survival, and then drinks the hemlock.

works.title: Phaedrus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on love, rhetoric and the soul
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates and Phaedrus talk beneath a plane-tree by the Ilissus: three speeches on love lead to the myth of the soul's winged chariot, and then to the nature of true rhetoric and the worth of writing.

works.title: Phaedrus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on love, rhetoric and the soul
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates and Phaedrus talk beneath a plane-tree by the Ilissus: three speeches on love lead to the myth of the soul's winged chariot, and then to the nature of true rhetoric and the worth of writing.

works.title: Philebus
works.subtitle: Socrates and Protarchus on pleasure and the good life
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates takes up the quarrel between Philebus, who holds that pleasure is the good, and the claims of wisdom, and with young Protarchus he sorts pleasures true and false, pure and mixed, to judge which life, or what blend of the two, deserves first place.

works.title: Philebus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on pleasure and wisdom as the good
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates and Protarchus take up Philebus's claim that pleasure is the good, weighing it against mind and wisdom, and ranking the elements of the good life.

works.title: Protagoras
works.subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates meets the great sophist Protagoras at the house of Callias and asks whether virtue is one thing or many, and whether it can be taught.

works.title: Protagoras
works.subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates meets the great sophist Protagoras at the house of Callias and asks whether virtue is one thing or many, and whether it can be taught. Translated by W. R. M. Lamb for the Loeb Classical Library (Plato, vol. IV, 1924).

works.title: The Republic
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates and his companions in the Piraeus ask what justice is, and build in speech an ideal city and a just soul, ending with the myth of Er.

works.title: Sophist
works.subtitle: The dialogue on being and not-being
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Theodorus brings a stranger from Elea to Socrates, and with Theaetetus he hunts the sophist through a series of divisions, which forces a reckoning with the riddle of what is not.

works.title: Sophist
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Theodorus brings a stranger from Elea to Socrates, and with Theaetetus he hunts the sophist through a series of divisions, which forces a reckoning with the riddle of what is not.

works.title: Statesman
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the art of ruling, also called Politicus
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: The Eleatic Stranger, with the young Socrates, seeks the definition of the statesman by division, tells the myth of the reversed cosmos, and likens the king's art to weaving.

works.title: Statesman
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the art of ruling, also called Politicus
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: The Eleatic Stranger, with the Younger Socrates, seeks the definition of the statesman by division, tells the myth of the reversed cosmos, and likens the king's art to weaving.

works.title: Symposium
works.subtitle: The banquet at Agathon's house and the speeches in praise of Love
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: At a supper in the house of the tragic poet Agathon, the guests, Socrates among them, each deliver a speech in praise of Love; the drunken Alcibiades breaks in at the end.

works.title: Symposium
works.subtitle: The banquet at Agathon's house and the speeches in praise of Love
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: At a supper in the house of the tragic poet Agathon, the guests, Socrates among them, each deliver a speech in praise of Love; the drunken Alcibiades breaks in at the end. Translated by W. R. M. Lamb for the Loeb Classical Library (Plato, vol. III, 1925).

works.title: Theaetetus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the nature of knowledge
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates, the midwife of ideas, questions the young Theaetetus on what knowledge is: perception, true opinion, or true opinion with an account.

works.title: Theaetetus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the nature of knowledge
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Socrates, the midwife of ideas, questions the young Theaetetus on what knowledge is: perception, true opinion, or true opinion with an account.

works.title: Timaeus
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Timaeus tells how a good Creator shaped the ordered world, its soul and its living creatures, after Socrates recalls the ideal state and Critias recalls the story of Atlantis.

works.title: Timaeus
works.subtitle: The dialogue on the making of the world, the soul and the human body
works.author: Plato
works.blurb: Timaeus tells how a good Creator shaped the ordered world, its soul and its living creatures, after Critias recalls the story of Atlantis.

works.title: Amphitryon
works.subtitle: Jupiter in Disguise
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: Jupiter takes the shape of the Theban general Amphitryon, and Mercury that of his slave Sosia, so that the god may spend the night with Alcmena while her husband is at the wars; when the true master and servant come home, nobody in the house can tell who is who, until Jupiter shows himself and Alcmena has borne twins, Hercules and Iphiclus.

works.title: Aulularia; or, The Concealed Treasure
works.subtitle: The Pot of Gold
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of Euclio, a miser who has found a pot of gold hidden by his grandfather and cannot rest for fear of thieves, while a rich neighbour asks for his daughter's hand, a slave steals the pot, and the girl's secret comes out. The ending is lost. Molière drew on it for L'Avare.

works.title: Bacchides; or, The Twin-Sisters
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: Mnesilochus asks his friend Pistoclerus to find his lost mistress Bacchis, and Pistoclerus is drawn into the house of her twin sister, also called Bacchis; the quick-witted slave Chrysalus then tricks old Nicobulus out of his gold, not once but twice, to rescue the young men from a swaggering captain. When the fathers finally see through the scheme and come to demand their sons, the two courtesans coax them in as well.

works.title: Captivi
works.subtitle: The Captives
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of two captives who swap names and clothes, so that a slave may send his master home, while the old man who owns them does not know that the slave is his own lost son.

works.title: Casina
works.subtitle: The Stratagem Defeated
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: Two slaves, Olympio the bailiff and Chalinus the armour-bearer, are set to win the foundling girl Casina as a bride, each at the secret bidding of a rival in love: old Stalino wants her for himself, and his son for himself. His wife Cleostrata takes her son's side, the matter is settled by drawing lots, and when Stalino's man wins she and her friend Myrrhina dress up Chalinus as the veiled bride, so that the old lecher and the bailiff go off to the bridal chamber with a bearded, hard-fisted wife; the play ends in a thrashing, a pardon, and the discovery that Casina is a freeborn Athenian.

works.title: Menaechmi
works.subtitle: The Twin Brothers
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of mistaken identity: one twin, carried off as a child to Epidamnus, is mistaken for the other, who has come in search of him, so that a courtesan, a parasite, a wife and a father-in-law all take the stranger for the man they know. It was the source of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors.

sections.title: Act V, Scene I (second Act V heading)
Act V, Scene II (second Act V heading)

works.title: Miles Gloriosus
works.subtitle: The Braggart Captain
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of Ephesus in which a vainglorious soldier who has carried off an Athenian girl is outwitted by his own slave: a hole in the party wall, a twin sister who does not exist, a pretended wife next door, and a beating for the braggart in the end.

works.title: Mostellaria
works.subtitle: The Haunted House
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: While old Theuropides is abroad, his son Philolaches squanders the estate on revels and on buying a music-girl her freedom; when the father returns unexpectedly, the quick-witted slave Tranio saves the day by claiming that the house is haunted and has been shut up, then ensnares the old man in one lie after another until the truth comes out and the young men are forgiven.

works.title: Pseudolus
works.subtitle: The Cheat
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of intrigue: the slave Pseudolus promises his young master Calidorus that he will win back the girl Phoenicium, whom the pimp Ballio has sold to a soldier, and he does it by tricking pimp, soldier's messenger and his own master alike. Cicero records that Plautus himself counted it among his best plays.

works.title: Rudens
works.subtitle: The Rope
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of shipwreck and recognition: a storm raised by the star Arcturus wrecks a procurer's ship off the coast near Cyrene and casts two girls ashore at the temple of Venus, where a fisherman hauls up in his net a wallet whose trinkets reveal that one of them is the lost daughter of the old exile who lives next door.

works.title: Trinummus
works.subtitle: The Three Pieces of Money
works.author: Plautus
works.blurb: A comedy of money and friendship, adapted from Philemon's The Treasure. While the merchant Charmides is abroad, his spendthrift son Lesbonicus sells the family house, and Charmides' friend Callicles buys it, in secret, to protect the treasure buried beneath it. To give the daughter a dowry without shaming her brother, a hired sharper is sent with a pretended letter and 'three pieces of money'; but Charmides returns just in time to meet him. The play opens with Luxury leading her daughter Poverty to the young man's door.

works.title: The Plays of Roswitha
works.subtitle: Gallicanus, Dulcitius, Callimachus, Abraham, Paphnutius, Sapientia
works.author: Hrotsvit of Gandersheim
works.blurb: Six saints' plays in Latin by a tenth-century Saxon canoness, written in answer to the comedies of Terence, in a lively English version of 1923.

works.title: The Pleasures of Memory
works.subtitle: In Two Parts
works.author: Samuel Rogers
works.blurb: Samuel Rogers's best-known poem, in heroic couplets, on the association of ideas and the consolations of memory, from a revisited village to the afterlife.

works.title: The Natural History, Volume I: Books I–V
works.subtitle: Books I–V
works.author: Pliny the Elder
works.translator: trans. John Bostock and H. T. Riley (1855)
works.blurb: Pliny's vast encyclopaedia of the natural world, in the Bohn translation: the dedication and contents, then cosmology and the heavens (Book II) and the geography of Europe, Africa and Asia (Books III–V).

works.title: Letters
works.subtitle: Selected letters, with the correspondence with the Emperor Trajan
works.author: Pliny the Younger
works.translator: trans. William Melmoth (1746), revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet (1878)
works.blurb: Pliny's polished letters to friends and statesmen, among them the eruption of Vesuvius and his ghost stories, followed by his official correspondence with the Emperor Trajan, including the exchange on the Christians of Bithynia.

works.subtitle: The Ethical Treatises
works.author: Plotinus
works.blurb: The nine ethical treatises that open Porphyry's arrangement of Plotinus, on the soul and the man, virtue, dialectic, happiness, beauty, the Good and the nature of evil.

works.author: Plotinus
works.blurb: The nine treatises of the Second Ennead, on the heavens and the stars, matter, potentiality and actuality, quality, and the argument against the Gnostics, in Stephen MacKenna's English of 1921.

works.author: Plotinus
works.blurb: The nine treatises of the Third Ennead, on fate and providence, our tutelary spirit, love, the impassivity of the unembodied, time and eternity, and contemplation, in Stephen MacKenna's English of 1921.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Demetrius and Antony
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs two flamboyant and ill-fated men of power, Demetrius the City-besieger, successor of Alexander, and Mark Antony, the Roman general. He offers them as cautionary examples, men whose great gifts were undone by pleasure and passion. Demetrius's sieges, kingship and fall in Macedonia and Asia are set beside Antony's rise under Caesar, the triumvirate, Cleopatra, Actium and death in Alexandria.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Demosthenes and Cicero
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the greatest Greek orator beside the greatest Roman one. Demosthenes rises from a plundered orphanhood and a stammering tongue to lead Athens against Philip and Alexander of Macedon, and dies by poison rather than fall into Antipater's hands. Cicero climbs from a provincial family to the consulship, crushes the conspiracy of Catiline, is driven into exile, and is finally hunted down and killed on the orders of Antony.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Agesilaus and Pompey
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the Spartan king Agesilaus, who led Greek arms into Asia and ruled Sparta for decades, beside Pompey the Great, the Roman general whose victories over pirates and eastern kings ended in defeat by Caesar and a murder on the Egyptian shore. Both men gained great fame, and both were brought low by the fortunes of civil strife. A short comparison closes the pair.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Agis and Cleomenes, Tiberius and Caius Gracchus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs the Spartan reforming kings Agis IV and Cleomenes III with the Roman tribunes Tiberius and Caius Gracchus, four idealists who tried to restore a lost equality of land and citizenship and died for it. The closing Comparison sets the two pairs side by side, weighing the Romans' fine upbringing against the Spartans' bolder remedies.

sections.title: Comparison of Agis and Cleomenes with the Gracchi

works.title: Parallel Lives: Alcibiades and Coriolanus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs the brilliant, unstable Athenian Alcibiades with the Roman patrician Coriolanus. Each is a gifted soldier whose pride and anger drive him from his city into the camp of its enemies. Alcibiades' career runs from his youth under Socrates through the Sicilian expedition, exile and recall; Coriolanus' from his valour at Corioli to his banishment and his march on Rome. A short comparison weighs the two.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Alexander and Caesar
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs the conqueror Alexander the Great with Julius Caesar, who overthrew Pompey. Declaring that he writes lives, not histories, he looks to a phrase or a jest for the signs of the soul. Alexander's youth, his campaigns from the Granicus to Babylon and his death are set beside Caesar's rise, the Gallic wars, the civil war against Pompey and the Ides of March.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Aratus, Artaxerxes, Galba and Otho
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Four single Lives from the later part of Plutarch's series. Aratus recounts the Achaean statesman who freed Sicyon and built up the Achaean League against Macedon. Artaxerxes follows the Persian king Artaxerxes II, his rivalry with his brother Cyrus, and the intrigues of the court. Galba and Otho tell of the Roman emperors of the civil-war year that followed Nero's death.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Aristides and Cato the Elder
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the incorruptible Athenian Aristides, called the Just, beside Marcus Cato the Censor, the stern guardian of old Roman ways. Both men rose by character rather than birth, and both are shown as champions of probity at the cost of popularity. The pair closes with a formal comparison of the two statesmen.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Cimon and Lucullus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs Cimon, the Athenian statesman and general who won the victories at the Eurymedon and carried the war against Persia, with Lucullus, the Roman commander who defeated Mithridates and Tigranes and then retired to a famous luxury. The two lives are closed by a short comparison of the men.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Dion and Brutus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs Dion of Syracuse, Plato's disciple who overthrew the tyrant Dionysius, with Marcus Brutus, who led the conspiracy against Caesar. Both were pupils of Plato's philosophy, both were cut off before their aims were achieved, and each saw an ill-boding spectre before the end. Dion's exile, return and murder are set beside Brutus's part in the Ides of March and his defeat at Philippi, with a brief closing comparison.

works.title: Parallel Lives, Part I
works.subtitle: Theseus to Marcus Cato, with their Comparisons
works.author: Plutarch
works.translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the lives of Greek and Roman statesmen and soldiers side by side, reading character through deeds, sayings and small incidents, and closes most pairs with a comparison of the two men. This first part opens with the founders and lawgivers, Theseus and Romulus, Lycurgus and Numa, Solon and Poplicola, then follows the great captains and politicians of Athens and Rome, among them Themistocles, Pericles, Alcibiades, Coriolanus, Aemilius Paulus and Cato the Censor.

sections.title: Comparison of Timoleon with Aemilius Paulus
Comparison of Aristides with Marcus Cato

works.title: Parallel Lives, Part II
works.subtitle: Philopoemen to Pompey and Agesilaus, with their Comparisons
works.author: Plutarch
works.translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
works.blurb: The second part of the Lives pairs Greek and Roman soldiers and statesmen of the Hellenistic and late Republican ages: Philopoemen and Flamininus, the liberators and last defenders of Greece; Pyrrhus and Marius; Lysander and Sylla; Cimon and Lucullus; Nicias and Crassus, two fortunes ruined abroad; Sertorius and Eumenes, exiles who led foreign armies; and Agesilaus and Pompey. As before, Plutarch reads character through deeds and sayings, and closes most pairs with a comparison.

works.title: Parallel Lives, Part III
works.subtitle: Alexander to Cicero, with their Comparisons
works.author: Plutarch
works.translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
works.blurb: Here Plutarch pairs the conquerors and the statesmen who failed to save their republics: Alexander with Caesar, the honest Phocion with Cato the Younger, the reforming kings of Sparta, Agis and Cleomenes, with the tribunes Tiberius and Caius Gracchus, and finally the orator Demosthenes with Cicero. Anecdote, omen and last words are his preferred evidence of character.

sections.title: Comparison of Tiberius and Caius Gracchus with Agis and Cleomenes

works.title: Parallel Lives, Part IV
works.subtitle: Demetrius to Otho, with their Comparisons
works.author: Plutarch
works.translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
works.blurb: The last part of the Lives pairs Demetrius the Besieger with Mark Antony, Dion of Syracuse with Marcus Brutus, and closes with the single Lives of Aratus of Sicyon, the Persian king Artaxerxes, and the short-lived emperors Galba and Otho. Plutarch reads ambition, luxury and loyalty through the fates of men who rose by arms and fell to their own excess or to conspiracy, from the Hellenistic kings to the civil wars of Rome and the year of the four emperors.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Lycurgus and Numa
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus with Numa Pompilius, the pious second king of Rome. Both are shadowy figures whose dates and deeds are disputed, and both gave their cities the laws and institutions that shaped them. Lycurgus's austere discipline of land, table and training for war is set beside Numa's calendar, priesthoods and cult of peace, and a closing Comparison weighs the two statesmen against each other.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Lysander and Sulla
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the Spartan admiral Lysander, who broke Athens at Aegospotami and then overreached at home, beside Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman general who won the civil war, took the dictatorship and wrote his own epitaph. The two Lives follow ambition, luck and cruelty in victory, and the closing Comparison weighs Lysander's self-restraint against Sulla's greater successes.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Nicias and Crassus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs Nicias, the cautious Athenian general whose scruples and superstition doomed the Sicilian expedition, with Crassus, the richest man in Rome, whose greed for glory ended in the Parthian disaster at Carrhae. Warning that Thucydides has already told the Sicilian story unsurpassably, he follows with a closing comparison of the two fortunes and the two men.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Pelopidas and Marcellus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the Theban liberator Pelopidas beside the Roman general Marcellus, finding in both a valour that risked too much. Pelopidas overthrows the Spartan garrison of Thebes, leads the Sacred Band at Leuctra and dies fighting the tyrant Alexander of Pherae. Marcellus wins the spolia opima, takes Syracuse despite the engines of Archimedes and falls in an ambush near Hannibal's camp. A short comparison weighs the two.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Pericles and Fabius Maximus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs the Athenian statesman Pericles, who made Athens the school of Hellas, with Fabius Maximus, the cautious Roman dictator who wore Hannibal down by delay. He opens by urging that we study virtuous lives rather than idle spectacles, then follows Pericles from the Parthenon to the plague, and Fabius from the Alps to the walls of Tarentum, closing with a formal comparison of the two.

sections.title: Comparison of Pericles and Fabius Maximus

works.title: Parallel Lives: Philopoemen and Flamininus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs Philopoemen, the Achaean general whom he calls the last of the Greeks, with Titus Flamininus, the Roman who proclaimed freedom for Greece at the Isthmian Games after defeating Philip V of Macedon. Philopoemen reforms the Achaean army, defeats the Spartan tyrant Machanidas and dies a prisoner of the Messenians; Flamininus wins at Cynoscephalae, wars against Nabis, and brings about the flight of Hannibal. A brief comparison weighs the two.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Phocion and Cato the Younger
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs Phocion, the austere Athenian general who was elected strategos forty-five times and yet was put to death by the city he served, with Cato the Younger, the unbending Roman Stoic who killed himself at Utica rather than live under Caesar. Both men were honest in a corrupt age and both were destroyed by it. No formal Comparison of the two survives.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Pyrrhus and Caius Marius
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the Epirot king Pyrrhus beside the Roman general Caius Marius. Pyrrhus, kinsman of Alexander, wins his famous costly victories against Rome in Italy and Sicily and dies in the streets of Argos. Marius, a peasant's son from Arpinum, rises to a record seven consulships, defeats Jugurtha and the Cimbri and Teutones, then is drawn into civil war with Sulla. Both are portrayed as brilliant soldiers whose restless ambition outran their fortune.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Sertorius and Eumenes
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs two exiles who led armies of foreigners: the Roman Sertorius, who held Spain against Sulla's successors and Pompey until his own officers murdered him, and Eumenes of Cardia, Alexander's secretary, who fought the Successors until betrayed to Antigonus. Plutarch opens with a meditation on coincidence, and closes with a short comparison of the two men's careers and deaths.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Solon and Publicola
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch sets the Athenian lawgiver Solon beside Publicola, the Roman who helped drive out the Tarquins and stood first among the founders of the Republic. Solon's cancelling of debts, his laws, his poems and his meeting with Croesus are matched with Publicola's consulship, his laws and his wars against Tarquin and Porsena, and a closing comparison weighs the two men.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Themistocles and Camillus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs the Athenian Themistocles, architect of the fleet that won Salamis, with Camillus, the Roman who saved the city from the Gauls. Each statesman is driven into exile by the ingratitude of his own people, and each is shown in the hour of the country's peril. The comparison of the pair is lost.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Theseus and Romulus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch pairs Theseus, the legendary founder of Athens, with Romulus, the founder of Rome. Warning that the earliest ages shade into fable, he sets the Athenian's labours against the Roman's rise from the wolf's den to the walls of the city, and closes with a formal comparison of the two founders.

works.title: Parallel Lives: Timoleon and Aemilius Paulus
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Plutarch opens with his celebrated preface on why he writes Lives, using history as a mirror for his own conduct, and pairs two commanders whom fortune and wisdom favoured alike. Timoleon of Corinth frees Syracuse from the tyrants and defeats the Carthaginians at the Crimisus; Aemilius Paulus, a stern and upright Roman, conquers Perseus of Macedon at Pydna. A brief comparison weighs the two.

works.title: Moralia, Volume I
works.subtitle: Translated by Frank Cole Babbitt (Loeb Classical Library)
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Five essays from Plutarch's Moralia in Frank Cole Babbitt's Loeb translation, vol. I (1927): on bringing up children, reading the poets, listening to lectures, telling a flatterer from a friend, and judging one's own moral progress.

sections.title: How the Young Man Should Study Poetry
How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend
How a Man May Become Aware of His Progress in Virtue

works.title: Moralia, Volume II
works.subtitle: Translated by Frank Cole Babbitt (Loeb Classical Library)
works.author: Plutarch
works.blurb: Nine more essays from Plutarch's Moralia in Frank Cole Babbitt's Loeb translation, vol. II (1928): profiting from enemies, having many friends, chance, virtue and vice, a letter of condolence to Apollonius, keeping well, advice to a bride and groom, the dinner of the Seven Wise Men, and superstition.

sections.title: How to Profit by One’s Enemies
The Dinner of the Seven Wise Men

works.title: Essays and Miscellanies (Moralia), Volume I
works.subtitle: Translated from the Greek by Several Hands, corrected and revised by William W. Goodwin

works.translator: trans. Several hands, revised by William W. Goodwin (1870)
works.blurb: Seventeen of Plutarch's moral essays in the old English version of 1684-94, revised by William Goodwin: on bringing up children, curing anger and bashfulness, the peace of the mind, superstition, music, health, marriage, friendship, grief and the Spartan way of life, with the sayings of kings and the orations on Alexander.

works.title: Essays and Miscellanies (Moralia), Volume II
works.subtitle: Translated from the Greek by Several Hands, corrected and revised by William W. Goodwin
works.author: Plutarch
works.translator: trans. several hands, revised by William W. Goodwin (1870)
works.blurb: Seventeen more of Plutarch's moral essays in the old English version of 1684-94, revised by William Goodwin: the Banquet of the Seven Wise Men, how a young man ought to hear poems, envy and hatred, the flatterer and the friend, against Epicurus, the Roman and Greek Questions, the love of wealth, the soul in Plato's Timaeus, Socrates's daemon, curiosity, progress in virtue, fortune, and conjugal precepts.

works.title: Essays and Miscellanies (Moralia), Volume III
works.subtitle: Translated from the Greek by Several Hands, corrected and revised by William W. Goodwin
works.author: Plutarch
works.translator: trans. Several hands, revised by William W. Goodwin (1870)
works.blurb: Ten of Plutarch's essays in the old English version of 1684-94, revised by William Goodwin: on living unnoticed, exile, brotherly love, Aristophanes and Menander, the verse of the Delphic oracles, the opinions of the philosophers on nature, the Stoics, moral virtue, and the long table-talk of the Symposiacs and the Natural Questions.

works.title: Poemi conviviali
works.author: Giovanni Pascoli
works.blurb: Pascoli's cycle of Hellenic and ancient-world poems, written as if recited at a symposium: Solon, the blind Homer, Achilles' lyre, the last voyage of Odysseus, Alexander, Tiberius and the Nativity.

works.blurb: Twelve of the prose poems in the English of Arthur Symons, who introduced Baudelaire’s Paris to English readers: the moon’s caprice, the eyes of the poor, a doomed buffoon, and the command to be drunken.

works.title: The Poetic Edda
works.subtitle: Lays of the Gods and Lays of the Heroes, translated from the Icelandic with the stanza numbering of the standard editions
works.author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
works.blurb: The great Old Norse collection of mythological and heroic lays preserved in the Codex Regius, in Bellows's 1923 verse translation, with the Eddas' own prose links kept in place.

works.title: Eddukvæði
works.subtitle: Völuspá, from the Old Norse text of Sophus Bugge (1867) in normalised spelling
works.author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
works.blurb: The Old Norse text of the Eddic lays, as edited by Sophus Bugge in 1867 and set in normalised spelling. This edition so far contains Völuspá, the Seeress's prophecy of the making, doom and rebirth of the world.

works.title: The Elder Edda
works.subtitle: The Poetic Edda of Sæmund
works.author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
works.blurb: The Old Norse mythological and heroic lays of the Codex Regius in Benjamin Thorpe's 1866 prose translation, with the manuscripts' own prose links kept in place.

works.title: The Poet's Pilgrimage to Waterloo
works.subtitle: Proem and two parts (1816)
works.author: Robert Southey
works.blurb: Southey's account in six-line stanzas of his journey in 1815 through Flanders and Brussels to the field of Waterloo, followed by a dream-vision on the Mountain of the Muse in which he is shown the hopes of mankind after the victory.

sections.title: Part I, Canto III: The Field of Battle
Part I, Canto IV: The Scene of War

works.title: Politian: Scenes from an Unpublished Drama
works.author: Edgar Allan Poe
works.blurb: Poe's only drama, left unfinished, survives in five blank-verse scenes set in Rome. Politian, Earl of Leicester, loves Lalage, a ward whose betrothal to the Count Castiglione stands in the way; haunted by melancholy and fatal premonition, he is drawn toward a challenge that the scenes break off before resolving.

works.title: Poltava
works.subtitle: A poem in three cantos
works.author: Alexander Pushkin
works.blurb: Pushkin's narrative poem of Mazeppa, Kotzubei and his daughter Marie, set against the Ukrainian hetman's betrayal of Peter the Great and the battle of Poltava (1709), in Charles Edward Turner's 1899 English version.

works.title: Poly-Olbion
works.subtitle: A Chorographicall Description of Great Britain, in thirty Songs
works.author: Michael Drayton
works.blurb: Drayton's topographical poem in alexandrines on the rivers, hills, forests and history of England and Wales, in thirty Songs (Songs 1-18 printed 1612, Songs 19-30 in 1622), each opening with its verse Argument; Selden's prose Illustrations are omitted.

works.title: The Histories, Books I–IX
works.author: Polybius
works.blurb: Polybius's account of how Rome came to rule the Mediterranean world in barely fifty-three years, from the First Punic War to the fall of Carthage, with his famous analysis of the Roman constitution in Book VI.

works.title: The Histories, Books X–XL and fragments
works.author: Polybius
works.blurb: The surviving later books of Polybius's history of Rome's rise, from the recovery of Tarentum and Scipio in Spain through Cannae's aftermath, Zama, the wars with Philip, Antiochus and Perseus, to the destruction of Carthage and Corinth in 146 BC, with his reflections on historical method and his own conclusion.

works.title: The Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians
works.author: Polycarp of Smyrna
works.blurb: A short pastoral letter from the bishop of Smyrna to the church at Philippi, on righteousness, the duties of deacons and presbyters, and the example of the martyrs.

works.title: Polyeucte
works.author: Pierre Corneille
works.blurb: Polyeucte, an Armenian nobleman newly converted to Christianity, is married to Pauline, who once loved the Roman knight Severus and obeyed her father in marrying another. When Severus returns in favour with the Emperor, Polyeucte's zeal leads him to smash the pagan idols and refuse to recant, even at the pleading of his wife and father-in-law. His martyrdom in turn converts Pauline and, finally, her father Felix. Corneille's tragedy of 1643 is written in rhymed couplets.

sections.title: Act IV: Polyeucte, Cleon, Three Other Guards

works.title: Τὰ μεθ' Ὅμηρον (Ta meth' Homeron)
works.author: Quintus Smyrnaeus
works.blurb: The Greek text of the Posthomerica, Quintus Smyrnaeus's fourteen-book hexameter continuation of the Iliad, from the funeral of Hector through the deaths of Akhilleus, Paris and Penthesileia, the wooden horse and the sack of Troy, to the Greeks' storm-wrecked voyage home. Each book pairs with the same-numbered book of Way's English translation, The Fall of Troy.

works.title: Garrick's Looking-Glass; or, the Art of Rising on the Stage
works.subtitle: A Poem in Three Cantos
works.author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
works.blurb: A satirical poem in three cantos on the theatrical world of David Garrick, published in 1776 (TCP K040357).

works.title: Humanity, or the Rights of Nature
works.subtitle: A Poem in Two Books
works.author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
works.blurb: Pratt’s verse attack on the slave trade and on cruelty to the weak, in heroic couplets, published in 1788 (TCP K038048).

works.title: Sympathy; or, a Sketch of the Social Passion
works.subtitle: A Poem
works.author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
works.blurb: A two-book poem in praise of fellow-feeling as the bond of society, published in 1781 (TCP K094645).

works.title: Prince Arthur
works.subtitle: An Heroick Poem in Ten Books
works.author: Sir Richard Blackmore
works.blurb: Blackmore's first epic, in ten books of rhymed couplets, follows the British prince Arthur against the Saxons, with Lucifer and the powers of Hell working to thwart him.

works.title: Prince Hohenstiel-Schwangau, Saviour of Society
works.author: Robert Browning
works.blurb: A dramatic monologue in blank verse in which a disgraced ruler, a thinly veiled Napoleon III, defends his career to a woman in London.

works.title: The Prince's Quest
works.author: William Watson
works.blurb: A romance in ten parts of a prince who sets out in search of the meaning of life and love, written in rhymed couplets.

works.title: Princess Ida
works.subtitle: Or, Castle Adamant
works.author: W. S. Gilbert
works.blurb: Prince Hilarion was betrothed in infancy to Princess Ida, daughter of the crabbed King Gama. Ida has withdrawn to Castle Adamant, a women's university where men are forbidden. Hilarion and his friends Cyril and Florian infiltrate it in disguise, and Gilbert's 'respectful perversion' of Tennyson's The Princess turns the quarrel into a comedy of learning, vanity and love.

works.title: History of the Wars: The Gothic War, Books V–VI
works.subtitle: The Gothic War, from the fall of the Western Empire to the siege of Rome
works.author: Procopius
works.blurb: Procopius's eyewitness account of Belisarius's war against the Ostrogoths in Italy, from the deposition of Romulus Augustulus to the siege of Rome, in H. B. Dewing's English prose of 1919.

works.title: History of the Wars, Books I–II: The Persian War
works.subtitle: Justinian's wars with Persia, from the reign of Arcadius to the plague of 542
works.author: Procopius
works.blurb: The first two books of Procopius's history of Justinian's wars: the long conflict between Rome and Persia, the Nika riot of 532 and Belisarius's early commands, and the invasion of Chosroes in the following decade.

works.title: History of the Wars, Books III-IV: The Vandalic War
works.author: Procopius
works.blurb: Procopius of Caesarea's account of Justinian's reconquest of North Africa from the Vandals under Belisarius, from the Vandal migrations and the fall of Carthage to the Moorish revolts and the mutiny of Stotzas.

works.title: Προμηθεὺς δεσμώτης (Prometheus desmotes)
works.author: Aeschylus
works.blurb: The Greek text of this tragedy by Aeschylus in the Smyth Loeb edition, set out by episode and choral division, so that it can be read beside the English verse translation of the same play.

works.title: Prometheus Bound
works.author: Aeschylus
works.blurb: For giving fire to mortals against the will of Zeus, the Titan Prometheus is nailed to a crag in the Scythian wastes by Strength and Force, while a reluctant Hephaestus does the work. Visited by the sea-nymphs, by Oceanus and by the wandering, cow-horned Io, he foretells the fall of Zeus, until Hermes comes to demand the secret and the rocks collapse upon him.

works.title: Prometheus the Firegiver
works.subtitle: A Mask in the Greek Manner
works.author: Robert Bridges
works.blurb: Prometheus comes down to Argos on a festival of Zeus and persuades the king Inachus to defy the god and accept the gift of fire, foretelling the fate of Inachus's daughter Io before he kindles the altar and writes his own name upon it in the place of Zeus. Bridges's mask, first printed privately at Oxford in 1883, follows the Greek manner, with a chorus of youths and maidens singing hymns to Zeus, an ode on wonder, a tragic hymn on the lot of man, and a final chorus in praise of the Firegiver.

works.title: Prometheus Unbound
works.subtitle: A Lyrical Drama in Four Acts
works.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
works.blurb: Shelley's lyrical drama in four acts, in which the Titan chained to the Caucasus is freed when Jupiter is overthrown and love takes the place of tyranny.

works.title: Prometidjon
works.subtitle: Rzecz w dwóch dialogach: Bogumił i Wiesław
works.author: Cyprian Kamil Norwid
works.blurb: Norwid's two dialogues in verse on art and truth: in Bogumił the speakers argue about the place of art, taking Chopin as their first example, and in Wiesław about truth, prophecy and the public voice.

Wiesław. Dialog, w którym jest rzecz o prawdzie, jej promieniach i duchu. Jako treść.

works.title: Psalm of the West
works.author: Sidney Lanier
works.blurb: Lanier's long poem on the making of America, running from Columbus's night voyage and the Norse landing in Vinland through the Mayflower and Lexington.

works.title: Psyche
works.subtitle: or, The Legend of Love
works.author: Mary Tighe
works.blurb: Mary Tighe's retelling of the myth of Cupid and Psyche, from Apuleius, in six cantos of Spenserian stanzas.

sections.title: Dedicatory Sonnet, Addressed to My Mother

works.title: The Instruction of Ptah-hotep and the Instruction of Ke'gemni
works.subtitle: The Oldest Books in the World
works.author: Ptah-hotep
works.blurb: The oldest surviving Egyptian books of counsel, in which a vizier instructs his son in speech, manners and justice.

works.title: Punica
works.subtitle: The Second Punick War between Hannibal and the Romanes
works.author: Silius Italicus
works.blurb: Silius Italicus's Latin epic of the war between Rome and Hannibal, the longest surviving Latin epic, in seventeen books of heroic couplets by Thomas Ross.

works.title: The Purgatorio (Okey)
works.subtitle: Prose translation by Thomas Okey (Temple Classics)
works.author: Dante Alighieri
works.blurb: Dante's climb of the mountain of Purgatory in Thomas Okey's plain, literal prose for the Temple Classics, printed in 1901 as the facing English of the Italian text.

works.title: The Purple Island
works.subtitle: or, The Isle of Man
works.author: Phineas Fletcher
works.blurb: The body of man allegorised as an island, its anatomy described in Spenserian-derived stanzas, and the war of the virtues and vices for it in the last cantos.

works.title: קהלת (Qohelet)
works.subtitle: Hebrew text of Qohelet, Westminster Leningrad Codex.
works.author: The Hebrew Bible
works.blurb: The reflections of Qohelet, the Preacher, on vanity, time and the limits of human wisdom, in the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex.

works.title: Queen Hynde
works.author: James Hogg
works.blurb: Hogg's long romance in six parts, in tetrameter couplets, of a legendary Queen of Scotland in the age of St Columba, and the Norse suitors who beset her.

works.title: Queen Mary: A Drama
works.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
works.blurb: Tennyson's historical drama of the reign of Mary Tudor, from her triumphant entry into London and the Wyatt rebellion to her marriage to Philip of Spain, the burning of Cranmer, the loss of Calais and her death, with the throne passing to Elizabeth.

works.title: The Queen's Wake
works.subtitle: A Legendary Poem
works.author: James Hogg
works.blurb: Hogg's legendary poem of a minstrel contest at Holyrood, where the bards of Scotland sing before Mary, Queen of Scots, in the first weeks after her return from France. Twelve of the seventeen songs are given, among them Kilmeny and The Witch of Fife, together with the framing narrative divided into the Introduction, the three Nights, and the interludes between the songs.

sections.title: Interlude before The Witch of Fife
Interlude after The Witch of Fife
Interlude before The Fate of Macgregor

works.title: The Quest of the Sangraal
works.author: Robert Stephen Hawker
works.blurb: Hawker's blank-verse narrative of King Arthur's knights setting out from Tintagel on the quest for the Holy Grail (the Sangraal), with Merlin's prophecy and the lots cast for the four quarters of the world.

works.title: The Institutio Oratoria
works.subtitle: The Education of an Orator
works.author: Quintilian
works.blurb: Quintilian's twelve-book education of the orator, from the first lessons of childhood to the ideal orator's character and style, with a celebrated survey of Greek and Roman authors.

works.title: The Raghuvamsa (The Story of Raghu's Line)
works.subtitle: Raghuvamsa
works.author: Kalidasa
works.blurb: Kalidasa's epic of the solar dynasty of Raghu, from King Dilipa's vow at the hermitage of Vasishtha through Rama's life and banishment of Sita to the decline of the line under the last king, Agnivarna.

works.title: रघुवंशम् (Raghuvamsha)
works.subtitle: The Dynasty of Raghu, in the original Sanskrit
works.author: Kalidasa
works.blurb: Kalidasa's epic of the solar dynasty of Raghu in nineteen cantos, from King Dilipa's service to the cow Nandini through Raghu's conquests, Aja's lament for Indumati and Rama's life and banishment of Sita, to the voluptuary Agnivarna, last of the line.

works.title: Ralph Roister Doister
works.author: Nicholas Udall
works.blurb: The vain braggart Ralph Roister Doister, egged on by the parasite Matthew Merygreeke, sets out to win the rich widow Christian Custance, who is already promised to the merchant Gawyn Goodlucke. His love letter is read aloud with the punctuation turned so that it insults her, his mock funeral and his gifts come to nothing, and in the end Custance and her maids beat off his assault on her house. Often called the first English comedy, the play follows Plautus and Terence but is set among English townsfolk, with songs and a closing prayer for the Queen.

works.title: The Ramayana
works.subtitle: The Epic of Rama, Prince of India, Condensed into English Verse
works.author: Valmiki
works.blurb: Romesh Chunder Dutt's condensed English rendering of the Sanskrit epic of Rama, in twelve books of rhymed couplets, from the bridal of Sita to the sacrifice of the horse and the recognition of Lava and Kusa. Published by J. M. Dent and Co., London, 1899.

works.title: रामायणम् (Ramayana)
works.subtitle: Bala Kanda and Ayodhya Kanda
works.author: Valmiki
works.year: traditional, c. 5th century BCE - 3rd century CE
works.blurb: The original Sanskrit of the epic of Rama, attributed to the sage Valmiki: the birth and youth of Rama in the Bala Kanda, and his exile from Ayodhya in the Ayodhya Kanda.

works.title: रामचरितमानस — बालकाण्ड (Ramcharitmanas, Balkand)
works.subtitle: The first sopan (book), in part: from the opening shlokas to Doha 35
works.author: Tulsidas
works.blurb: Tulsidas's Awadhi retelling of the Rama story, in the first book (Balkand) only, and only as far as the transcription goes: the opening shlokas and sorathas, then the chaupai groups and dohas through Doha 35.

sections.title: सोरठा 1–5 (जेहि सुमिरत सिधि होइ, गन-नायक करि-बर-बदन)
दोहा 2 (गुरु-पद-रज मृदु मञ्जुल अञ्जन। नयन-अमिय दृग दोष बिभञ्जन।)
दोहा 3 (मज्जन फल पेखिय ततकाला। काक होहिं पिक बकउ मराला)
दोहा 4 (बहुरिवन्दि खलगन सतिभाये। जे बिनु काज दाहिनेहुँ बाँये।)
दोहा 5 (में अपनी दिसि कीन्ह निहोरा। तिन्ह निज ओर न लाउब भोरा)
दोहा 6 (खल-अघ-अगुन साधु-गुन-गाहा। उभय अपार उदधि अवगाहा)
दोहा 7 (अस बिबेक जब देइ बिधाता। तब तजि दोष गुनहि मन राता)
दोहा 8 (आकर चारि लाख चौरासी। जाति जीव जल-थल-नभ-वासी)
दोहा 9 (खल परिहास होइ हित मोरा। काक कहहिं कलकंठ कठोरा)
दोहा 10 (एहि महँ रघुपति नाम उदारा। अति पावन पुरान-स्रुति-सारा)

दोहा 15 (पुनि बन्दउँ सारद सुरसरिता। जुगल पुनीत मनोहर-चरिता)
